profiles.meeting_scenario: At an academic medical center, a clinical epidemiologist and a regulatory intelligence lead are holding a brainstorming meeting for a follow-up cross sectional study on new medical devices reported in the literature from 2018-2022. The team wants to update an older published analysis by identifying devices first described in clinical studies, classifying device type and specialty, and determining whether FDA clearance or approval occurred before the first publication. The agenda is to generate a workable study frame, surface practical heuristics for matching publications to regulatory records, and sketch a pilot workflow. The expected outcome is a short list of candidate inclusion and linkage rules plus an agreed first-pass plan for a pilot sample.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: Systematic reviews, evidence synthesis, observational study design, publication timeline analysis
members.background: Lena is a physician-researcher who has led several literature-based studies on devices and diagnostics and is known for reproducible screening methods built around PubMed and protocolized abstraction.
members.private_state: She wants a study design that will be easy to preregister, defend in peer review, and hand off to research assistants without large amounts of subjective judgment.
hidden_assumptions: A 'new device' should be anchored to the first PubMed-indexed full clinical article on a specific named device model, not to broader platform history.
The relevant publication date is the earliest online citable date because that is when the evidence becomes publicly available.
For a cross sectional literature study, a public FDA master record is an adequate source for determining whether a device was cleared or approved.
If a paper does not name the exact marketed device or model, linking it to an FDA record is too inferential and should usually be avoided.

members.name: Ravi Menon
members.expertise: FDA device pathways, 510(k)/PMA/De Novo records, device naming conventions, commercialization timelines
members.background: Ravi previously worked in industry-facing regulatory strategy and now supports translational research teams by reconstructing approval histories across public FDA sources and sponsor documentation.
members.private_state: He wants the study to reflect how device programs actually evolve in practice, including rebranding, platform continuity, and pathway-specific records that are invisible in a simple literature abstraction.
hidden_assumptions: A 'new device' is best understood at the platform or product-family level, even if the marketed name changes between early studies and authorization.
The meaningful publication point is the journal issue or indexed publication record that clinicians and reviewers usually treat as the formal paper date.
There is no single FDA database for this purpose; valid ascertainment requires stitching together pathway-specific databases, summaries, and archived records.
Private-label versions, renamed models, and incremental generations often count as the same underlying device for regulatory linkage if the technical platform is continuous.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the 'first clinical study' of a new device
misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly refer to identifying the 'first clinical study' of each 'new device.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the first PubMed-indexed full human study of a specific named device model.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the first public clinical evidence tied to the same device platform or family, including renamed versions and sometimes early reports outside the exact later marketed model name.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase comes from the prior published study and sounds methodologically standard, so both assume they are inheriting the same convention without needing to unpack edge cases during brainstorming.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They say they will 'check the FDA database' for clearance or approval.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking mainly of a public master source such as Devices@FDA or the most visible FDA entry for a marketed product.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of a composite search across 510(k), PMA, De Novo, product code pages, summaries, and archived pathway-specific records.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In practice both professionals casually compress multiple FDA sources into the singular phrase 'the FDA database,' so the wording creates false consensus while masking different retrieval plans.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for approval to happen 'before publication'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss whether a device was 'cleared before publication.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 would compare the FDA decision date with the article's earliest online citable publication date.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 would compare the regulatory date with the formal journal issue or indexed publication date that is commonly treated as the paper's publication date.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Online-first and issue dates are often close together, so the phrase seems precise enough in ordinary conversation and the discrepancy only matters in borderline cases that do not arise explicitly in the meeting.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the 'same device' when linking papers to approvals
misalignment_points.surface_form: They talk about matching each paper to 'the same device' in FDA records.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the linkage should stay within the exact trade name or model explicitly stated in the publication.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the linkage can extend to relabeled versions, successor models, or the same technical platform across branding changes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both believe they are simply being careful about matching, but they draw the boundary of the device entity differently; this usually stays hidden until coders encounter ambiguous brand histories.

turns.inner_thought: I want this to look like a clean update of the older cross sectional paper, but with tighter reproducibility. The key is defining the first clinical study of each new device in a way an RA can execute from PubMed without subjective reconstruction. For me that means the first PubMed-indexed full human paper on a specifically named device model during 2018-2022, not a fuzzy lineage exercise.
turns.utterance: I was thinking we could do a follow-up cross sectional study for 2018 through 2022, basically updating the earlier analysis but with a more explicit workflow. We would identify devices first described in clinical papers, classify device type and specialty, and then look at whether they were cleared before publication. The first question is how we want to identify the first clinical study of each new device.

turns.inner_thought: A pilot will go faster if we choose areas with a mix of pathways and enough device turnover. Cardiology and orthopedics should surface the hard cases: renamed programs, incremental generations, private-label versions. When she says first clinical study of each new device, I assume we're talking about the earliest public clinical evidence for the underlying platform, even if the later marketed name isn't there yet.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. For a pilot, I’d probably start with cardiology and orthopedics because they should give us a good spread of devices and regulatory histories. For the first clinical study of each new device, I’d want us to trace it from its earliest clinical appearance and keep following it even if the name looks a little different later on.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with those specialties. I need a conservative screen: PubMed, full clinical studies, human subjects, protocolized abstraction. Then we check the FDA database for whether each named device was cleared or approved. For timing, I want the earliest online citable date because that's public availability and easy to extract consistently from the article record.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I’d prefer to keep the initial screen pretty conservative. We can build it around PubMed, pull full clinical studies in humans, and then abstract the first clinical study for each device from there. After that we can check the FDA database to see whether each one was cleared before publication.

turns.inner_thought: Good, I can handle the regulatory side. When I say the FDA database, I mean the whole patchwork: 510(k), PMA, De Novo, summaries, archived pages, product codes. That's exactly what we need if names shift across records. Same device should follow the platform across relabeling if the trail supports it.
turns.utterance: Agreed. And when we check the FDA database, we should be able to use that step to map the pathway as well, whether it’s 510(k), PMA, or De Novo. That will also help when the product naming shifts across records but it’s still the same device.

turns.inner_thought: I want to nail down the timing rule now so the variable doesn't get messy later. Earliest online article date is objective and usually in the citation metadata. If we stick to the first clinical study and use online-first, then cleared before publication becomes a straightforward binary comparison against the FDA decision date.
turns.utterance: For the timing piece, I think we can keep it fairly simple. If we use the earliest online article date, then the question of whether something was cleared before publication should be easy to code for the first study.

turns.inner_thought: I don't think the publication date will be a major issue; I usually rely on the journal record people cite and the indexed paper date. The bigger value is preserving the earliest clinical appearance of the platform, since early feasibility or first-in-human reports often predate the commercial name but still show when it entered the literature.
turns.utterance: That should be manageable. Publication timing is usually straightforward from the journal record, and on the front end I’d just make sure we don’t lose those early feasibility reports because they can still mark the first clinical study of a new device.

turns.inner_thought: This is where studies become unreviewable if we let interpretation creep in. I need a high-specificity linkage rule: if the exact device name or model isn't stated, we should usually exclude it rather than infer across branding history. Same device should mean what the paper explicitly names, otherwise the RA team will drift.
turns.utterance: One thing I’d like for the pilot is a fairly strict linkage rule. If the article doesn’t give us a clear device name, I’d rather treat it as ambiguous and leave it out, so that when we match the paper to the same device in FDA records the process stays reproducible.

turns.inner_thought: I get the reproducibility concern, but if we exclude everything with a naming wrinkle we'll miss how device programs actually move through authorization. We can still be systematic if we define continuity from the FDA trail. Same device can reasonably include relabeled versions or next-generation models when the technical platform is continuous and publicly traceable.
turns.utterance: I’m with you on reproducibility; I just think we can still get there without being overly narrow. In some cases, it may be appropriate to group relabeled versions or next-generation models under the same device if the FDA database shows a clear trail of continuity.

turns.inner_thought: I hear that as a secondary clean-up step, which is fine as long as the core workflow stays PubMed-first and coder-friendly. I'll keep the pilot structure simple: screen papers, identify the first clinical study for each device, abstract core fields, then look up approval status in the FDA database. We can review edge cases after the first pass.
turns.utterance: Okay, so maybe the pilot workflow is: PubMed screening first, abstract the first clinical study for each device, classify specialty and device type, and then pull clearance or approval status from the FDA database. We can keep notes on any difficult matches as we go.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. Once they send article-device pairs, I can reconstruct the pathway history and determine whether each one was cleared before publication using the regulatory record set I usually work with. I’ll also flag where the same device appears under different names so we don't misclassify continuity.
turns.utterance: That sounds like a good first pass. Once you have the first batch of article-device links, I can map the approval pathway on my end and flag which ones were cleared before publication, along with any cases where the same device shows up a little differently across the regulatory trail.
